results.title: Hyper-Leonardo numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $Le_n$ be the Leonardo numbers, defined by $Le_0 = Le_1 = 1$ and $Le_{n+2} = Le_{n+1} + Le_n + 1$. The hyper-Leonardo numbers are the integers $Le^{(r)}_n$, for $r, n \ge 0$, defined by $Le^{(0)}_n = Le_n$ and $Le^{(r+1)}_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} Le^{(r)}_k$.

results.title: Hyper-Leonardo numbers of order zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the hyper-Leonardo number $Le^{(0)}_n$ equals the Leonardo number $L_{1,n}$, the generalized Leonardo number with $k = 1$, given by $L_{1,0} = L_{1,1} = 1$ and $L_{1,n+2} = L_{1,n+1} + L_{1,n} + 1$.

results.title: Hyper-Leonardo numbers as partial sums
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $r$ and $n$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $Le^{(r+1)}_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} Le^{(r)}_k$.

results.title: First hyper-Leonardo numbers of order one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(1)}_n$ of order $1$ satisfy $Le^{(1)}_0 = 1$, $Le^{(1)}_1 = 2$, $Le^{(1)}_2 = 5$ and $Le^{(1)}_3 = 10$.

results.title: Hyper-Fibonacci numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The hyper-Fibonacci numbers $F^{(r)}_n$, for natural numbers $r$ and $n$, are the natural numbers defined by $F^{(0)}_n = F_n$, the $n$-th Fibonacci number (with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$), and $F^{(r+1)}_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} F^{(r)}_k$.

results.title: Hyper-Fibonacci numbers of order zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the hyper-Fibonacci number $F^{(0)}_n$ equals the $n$-th Fibonacci number $F_n$ (with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$).

results.title: Hyper-Fibonacci numbers as partial sums
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $r$ and $n$, the hyper-Fibonacci numbers $F^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $F^{(r+1)}_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} F^{(r)}_k$.

results.title: Small values of the hyper-Fibonacci numbers of order one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The hyper-Fibonacci numbers $F^{(1)}_n$ of order $1$ satisfy $F^{(1)}_0 = 0$, $F^{(1)}_1 = 1$, $F^{(1)}_2 = 2$ and $F^{(1)}_3 = 4$.

results.title: Recurrences for the hyper-Leonardo numbers of orders zero, one and two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $Le^{(0)}_0 = Le^{(0)}_1 = 1$, $Le^{(1)}_0 = 1$, $Le^{(1)}_1 = 2$, $Le^{(2)}_0 = 1$ and $Le^{(2)}_1 = 3$, and for every natural number $n \ge 2$,

results.title: Recurrence for the hyper-Leonardo numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $r$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ of order $r$ satisfy $Le^{(r)}_0 = 1$, $Le^{(r)}_1 = r + 1$ and, for every natural number $n \ge 2$, $Le^{(r)}_n = r + Le^{(r)}_{n-1} + Le^{(r)}_{n-2} + \binom{n+r-2}{r} + \sum_{j=1}^{r-1} j \binom{n+r-2-j}{r-j}$.

results.title: Recurrence across consecutive orders of hyper-Leonardo numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $r \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $Le^{(r)}_n = Le^{(r)}_{n-1} + Le^{(r-1)}_n$.

results.title: Consecutive hyper-Leonardo numbers of order one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(1)}_n$ of order $1$ satisfy $Le^{(1)}_{n+1} = Le^{(1)}_n + L_{1,n+1}$, where $L_{1,n}$ is the generalized Leonardo number with $k = 1$, that is, the Leonardo number $Le_n$.

results.title: Generating function of shifted binomial coefficients
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $r$, the formal power series $\sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{n+r}{r} t^n$ with integer coefficients satisfies $\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{n+r}{r} t^n\right)(1-t)^{r+1} = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}[[t]]$, that is, $\sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{n+r}{r} t^n = 1/(1-t)^{r+1}$.

results.title: The convolution of log-concave sequences is log-concave
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and $(y_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be sequences of positive real numbers that are log-concave, that is, $x_{j-1} x_{j+1} \le x_j^2$ and $y_{j-1} y_{j+1} \le y_j^2$ for every $j \ge 1$. Let $z_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} x_k y_{n-k}$ be their convolution. Then $z_{j-1} z_{j+1} \le z_j^2$ for every $j \ge 1$.

results.title: Generating function of the Leonardo numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $Le_n$ be the Leonardo numbers ($Le_0 = Le_1 = 1$ and $Le_{n+2} = Le_{n+1} + Le_n + 1$), and let $L(t) = \sum_{n \ge 0} Le_n t^n$ in the ring $\mathbb{Z}[[t]]$ of formal power series. Then $L(t)(1 - 2t + t^3) = 1 - t + t^2$ and $L(t)(1 - t - t^2)(1 - t) = 2(1 - t) - (1 - t - t^2)$.

results.title: Generating functions of the hyper-Leonardo numbers of orders one and two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the ring $\mathbb{Z}[[t]]$ of formal power series, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} Le^{(1)}_n t^n\right)(1 - 2t + t^3)(1 - t) = 1 - t + t^2$ and $\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} Le^{(2)}_n t^n\right)(1 - 2t + t^3)(1 - t)^2 = 1 - t + t^2$.

results.title: Generating function of the hyper-Leonardo numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $r$, the formal power series $\sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n t^n$ of the hyper-Leonardo numbers of order $r$ satisfies $\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n t^n\right)(1-2t+t^3)(1-t)^r = 1-t+t^2$ in $\mathbb{Z}[[t]]$, that is, $\sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n t^n = \frac{1-t+t^2}{(1-2t+t^3)(1-t)^r}$.

results.title: Hyper-Leonardo numbers in terms of hyper-Fibonacci numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $r$ and $n$, the hyper-Leonardo number $\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n$ and the hyper-Fibonacci number $F^{(r)}_{n+1}$ satisfy $\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n = 2F^{(r)}_{n+1} - \binom{n+r}{r}$ as integers.

results.title: Log-convexity and log-concavity of the Leonardo numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $Le_n$ be the Leonardo numbers ($Le_0 = Le_1 = 1$ and $Le_{n+2} = Le_{n+1} + Le_n + 1$). Then $Le_n^2 \le Le_{n-1} Le_{n+1}$ for $n = 1$ and $n = 3$, $Le_5^2 = Le_4 Le_6$, and $Le_{n-1} Le_{n+1} \le Le_n^2$ for $n = 2$, $n = 4$ and every $n \ge 6$.

results.title: Leonardo numbers are log-balanced at index three
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $Le_n$ be the Leonardo numbers ($Le_0 = Le_1 = 1$ and $Le_{n+2} = Le_{n+1} + Le_n + 1$). Then $Le_3^2 \le Le_2 Le_4$ and $\frac{Le_2}{2!} \cdot \frac{Le_4}{4!} \le \left(\frac{Le_3}{3!}\right)^2$, the second inequality in the real numbers. That is, $(Le_n)$ satisfies the log-convexity inequality at $n = 3$ and $(Le_n / n!)$ satisfies the log-concavity inequality at $n = 3$.

results.title: Log-convexity and log-concavity of the hyper-Leonardo numbers at index one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The hyper-Leonardo numbers $\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $\left(\mathrm{Le}^{(1)}_1\right)^2 \le \mathrm{Le}^{(1)}_0 \mathrm{Le}^{(1)}_2$, and for every natural number $r \ge 2$ they satisfy $\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_0 \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_2 \le \left(\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_1\right)^2$.

results.title: Eventual log-concavity of the hyper-Leonardo numbers of order one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n \ge 2$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(1)}_n$ of order $1$ satisfy $Le^{(1)}_{n-1} Le^{(1)}_{n+1} \le (Le^{(1)}_n)^2$.

results.title: Cassini-type identity for hyper-Leonardo numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $r \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $Le^{(r)}_{n-1} Le^{(r)}_{n+1} - (Le^{(r)}_n)^2 = Le^{(r)}_n Le^{(r-1)}_{n+1} - Le^{(r-1)}_n Le^{(r)}_{n+1}$.

results.title: Eventual log-concavity of the hyper-Leonardo numbers of positive order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $r \ge 1$ and $n \ge 2$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ of order $r$ satisfy $Le^{(r)}_{n-1} Le^{(r)}_{n+1} \le (Le^{(r)}_n)^2$.

results.title: Convexity of the hyper-Leonardo numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $r$ and $n \ge 1$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $2 \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n \le \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_{n-1} + \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_{n+1}$.

results.title: Reversed index
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The reverse of an index $(k_0, \dots, k_{d-1})$ is the index $(k_{d-1}, \dots, k_0)$ with the same entries in the opposite order.

results.title: Strictly increasing tuples
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a strictly increasing tuple of length $d$ is a tuple $(m_0, \dots, m_{d-1})$ of positive natural numbers with $m_0 < m_1 < \cdots < m_{d-1}$. These are the summation variables of the increasing multiple-zeta convention.

results.title: Admissibility in the increasing convention
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An index $(k_0, \dots, k_{d-1})$ is admissible in the increasing convention when its list of entries read in reverse order, $(k_{d-1}, \dots, k_0)$, is admissible: it is nonempty, its first element $k_{d-1}$ is at least two, and its other elements are positive. Since the entries of an index are positive, this says that the index is nonempty and its last entry is at least two.

results.title: Increasing admissibility is admissibility of the reverse
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: An index is admissible in the increasing convention (nonempty with last entry at least two) if and only if its reverse is admissible (nonempty with first entry at least two).

results.title: Entries of the reversed index
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k = (k_0, \dots, k_{d-1})$ be an index of depth $d$; its reverse also has depth $d$. For every $i < d$, the $i$-th entry of the reverse of $k$ is $k_{d-1-i}$.

results.title: Reversal of strictly increasing tuples
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $k$ be an index of depth $d$; its reverse also has depth $d$. Sending a strictly increasing tuple $(m_0, \dots, m_{d-1})$ of positive natural numbers to the reversed tuple $(m_{d-1}, \dots, m_0)$ is a bijection from the strictly increasing tuples of length $d$ onto the strictly decreasing tuples of length $d$, whose inverse again reverses the order of the coordinates.

results.title: Reversal preserves each summand
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k = (k_0, \dots, k_{d-1})$ be an index of depth $d$ and let $m = (m_0, \dots, m_{d-1})$ be a strictly increasing tuple of positive natural numbers. results.title: Narayana number
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For positive integers $n$ and $k$, the Narayana number $N(n, k)$ is the natural number $\lfloor \binom{n}{k}\binom{n}{k-1} / n \rfloor$.

results.title: Defining formula for the Narayana number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For positive integers $n$ and $k$, the Narayana number $N(n, k)$ satisfies $N(n, k) = \lfloor \binom{n}{k}\binom{n}{k-1} / n \rfloor$.

results.title: Second formula for the Narayana number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For positive integers $n$ and $k$, the Narayana number $N(n, k)$ satisfies $N(n, k) = \lfloor \binom{n-1}{k-1}\binom{n}{k-1} / k \rfloor$.

results.title: Narayana polynomial coefficients
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Narayana polynomial coefficients are the natural numbers $a(n, k)$, for natural numbers $n$ and $k$, given by $a(0, 0) = 1$, $a(0, k) = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, $a(n, 0) = 0$ for $n \ge 1$, and $a(n, k) = N(n, k)$ for $n, k \ge 1$, where $N(n, k)$ is the Narayana number. So row zero is $1$ and every positive row has zero constant term.

results.title: Narayana polynomial coefficients at positive indices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the Narayana polynomial coefficient in row $n + 1$ and degree $k + 1$ equals the Narayana number $N(n + 1, k + 1)$.

results.summary: For a natural number $a$, the $q$-integer is the integer polynomial $[a]_q = 1 + q + \dots + q^{a-1} = \sum_{i=0}^{a-1} q^i$; in particular $[0]_q = 0$.

results.title: Baker-Gill-Solovay: oracles separate and collapse P vs NP
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an oracle $O$, a function from bitstrings to booleans, write $\mathsf{P}^O$ and $\mathsf{NP}^O$ for the classes of decision problems decidable in polynomial time, respectively in nondeterministic polynomial time, by machines that may query $O$. There is an oracle $O$ such that $\mathsf{P}^O \ne \mathsf{NP}^O$, and there is an oracle $O$ such that $\mathsf{P}^O = \mathsf{NP}^O$.

results.title: An oracle separates NP from coNP
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is an oracle $O$, a function from bitstrings to booleans, such that $\mathrm{NP}^O$ differs from the class $\mathrm{coNP}^O$ of decision problems $L$ whose complement, the decision problem that accepts exactly the bitstrings that $L$ rejects, belongs to $\mathrm{NP}^O$.

part.title: Minimal deterministic automaton
api: States reached in the minimized DFA
The minimized DFA accepts the same language

results.title: Left quotients of continuation languages
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA, write $\delta^*(q, x)$ for the state $M$ reaches from the state $q$ by reading the word $x$, and let $L_M(q)$ be the language of words accepted by $M$ when started in $q$. For every state $q$ and every word $x$, the left quotient $\{z : xz \in L_M(q)\}$ of $L_M(q)$ by $x$ equals $L_M(\delta^*(q, x))$.

results.title: Residual reached by a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the minimized state of $x$ is the language accepted by $M$ starting from the state that $M$ reaches on reading $x$ from its start state, viewed as an element of the reachable residuals of $M$.

results.title: Left quotients as reachable residuals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$. The set of left quotients $\{z : xz \in L\}$ of $L$ by words $x$ equals the set of reachable residuals of $M$ (the languages accepted by $M$ from the states it reaches from its start state). The bijection from the first set to the second sends each language to itself.

results.title: Minimized DFA
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$. The minimized DFA of $M$ has as states the reachable residuals of $M$, that is, the languages accepted by $M$ from the states it reaches from its start state. Its start state is $L$; on a letter $a$ it moves from a state $K$ to the left quotient $\{z : az \in K\}$; and its accepting states are those that contain the empty word.

results.title: States reached in the residual-language DFA
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every language $L$ and every word $x$, the state that the residual-language DFA of $L$ reaches on reading $x$ is the left quotient $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$. This automaton has the left quotients of $L$ as states, start state $L$, transition from $K$ on a letter $a$ to $a^{-1}K$, and accepts $K$ when $K$ contains the empty word.

results.title: Evaluation in the minimized DFA agrees with the left-quotient automaton
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$, and consider the automaton whose states are the left quotients of $L$, with start state $L$, moving from $K$ on a letter $a$ to $\{z : az \in K\}$. For every word $x$, the state that the minimized DFA of $M$ reaches on $x$, carried to the left quotients of $L$ by the bijection that sends each language to itself, is the state that this automaton reaches on $x$.

results.title: States reached in the minimized DFA
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every DFA $M$ and every word $x$, the state that the minimized DFA of $M$ reaches on $x$ is the language accepted by $M$ from the state that $M$ reaches on $x$.

results.title: Transitions of the minimized DFA
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA. For every reachable residual $K$ of $M$ (a state of the minimized DFA of $M$) and every letter $a$, the minimized DFA of $M$ moves from $K$ on input $a$ to the left quotient $\{z : az \in K\}$ of $K$ by $a$.

results.title: Transitions of the minimized DFA on reached states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA, and for a word $x$ let $[x]$ be the language accepted by $M$ from the state that $M$ reaches on $x$. For every word $x$ and every letter $a$, the minimized DFA of $M$ moves from the state $[x]$ on input $a$ to the state $[xa]$.

results.title: The minimized DFA accepts the same language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every DFA $M$, the minimized DFA of $M$ accepts exactly the language accepted by $M$.

results.title: The residual-language DFA is accessible
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every language $L$, the residual-language DFA of $L$ is accessible. This automaton has as states the left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for words $x$, start state $L$, transition from $K$ on a letter $a$ to $a^{-1}K$, and accepts $K$ when $K$ contains the empty word.

results.title: The minimized DFA is accessible
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every DFA $M$, every state of the minimized DFA of $M$ is reached from its start state by reading some word.

results.title: Nerode classes and reachable residuals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ accepting the language $L$, there is a bijection from the Nerode classes of $L$ to the reachable residuals of $M$; it sends the class of a word $x$ to the left quotient $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$.

results.title: Reachable residuals of the minimized DFA
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$. The reachable residuals of the minimized DFA of $M$ and the reachable residuals of $M$ both form the set of left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ of $L$ by words $x$, and this is the bijection from the first set to the second that sends each language to itself.

results.title: When finite, the minimized DFA has as many states as there are Nerode classes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$. If the set of reachable residuals of $M$ (the states of the minimized DFA of $M$) and the set of Nerode classes of $L$ are both finite, then they have the same number of elements.

results.title: CSLib automata as Mathlib DFAs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A CSLib deterministic automaton $M$ on finite words is viewed as a Mathlib DFA with the same states, the same transition function, the same start state and the same set of accepting states as $M$.

results.title: Mathlib DFAs as CSLib automata
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A Mathlib DFA $M$ is viewed as a CSLib deterministic automaton on finite words with the same states, the same transition function, the same start state and the same set of accepting states as $M$.

results.title: Converting a CSLib automaton to a Mathlib DFA preserves its language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every deterministic automaton $M$ on finite words, the DFA with the same states, transition function, start state and accepting states as $M$ accepts exactly the language of $M$.

results.title: The Nerode congruence relates words with equal left quotients
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $x, y \in \Sigma^*$. Then $x$ and $y$ are related by the Nerode congruence of $L$, that is, $xz \in L \iff yz \in L$ for every word $z$, if and only if they are Nerode equivalent for $L$, that is, their left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ and $y^{-1}L$ are equal.

results.title: The residual language of a Nerode class
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. This is the map from the classes of the Nerode congruence of $L$ to the set $\{w^{-1}L : w \in \Sigma^*\}$ of residual languages of $L$ that sends the class of each word $x$ to $x^{-1}L$; it is well defined because Nerode-congruent words have the same left quotient.

results.title: Nerode classes are the residual languages
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. This is the bijection from the classes of the Nerode congruence of $L$ onto the set $\{x^{-1}L : x \in \Sigma^*\}$ of residual languages of $L$ that sends the class of each word $x$ to $x^{-1}L$.

results.title: The Nerode automaton is the residual-language automaton
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. Consider the canonical automaton of $L$ as a DFA: its states are the classes $[x]$ of the Nerode congruence of $L$, its start state is the class of the empty word, on a letter $a$ it goes from $[x]$ to $[xa]$, and its accepting states are the classes of words of $L$. Renaming each…

results.title: The canonical automaton of a DFA's language is its minimized DFA
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ accepting the language $L$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. Consider the canonical automaton of $L$ as a DFA: its states are the classes $[x]$ of the Nerode congruence of $L$, its start state is the class of the empty word, on a letter $a$ it goes from $[x]$ to $[xa]$, and its accepting states are the classes of words of…

results.title: Morphisms of DFAs
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be DFAs over the same alphabet with transition functions $\delta_M$ and $\delta_N$. A morphism from $M$ to $N$ is a map $f$ from the states of $M$ to the states of $N$ that sends the start state of $M$ to the start state of $N$, satisfies $f(\delta_M(q, a)) = \delta_N(f(q), a)$ for every state $q$ of $M$ and every symbol $a$, and such that each state $q$ of $M$ is accepting if and only if $f(q)$ is…

results.title: DFA morphisms commute with evaluation from a state
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $f$ is a morphism from a DFA $M$ to a DFA $N$, then for every state $q$ of $M$ and every word $x$, running $N$ on $x$ from $f(q)$ ends in the image under $f$ of the state reached by running $M$ on $x$ from $q$.

results.title: DFA morphisms commute with evaluation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $f$ is a morphism from a DFA $M$ to a DFA $N$, then for every word $x$, the state that $N$ reaches on input $x$ from its start state is the image under $f$ of the state that $M$ reaches on input $x$ from its start state.

results.title: DFA morphisms preserve the accepted language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $f$ is a morphism from a DFA $M$ to a DFA $N$ over the same alphabet, then $M$ and $N$ accept the same language.

results.title: Identity DFA morphism
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For every DFA $M$, the identity map on the states of $M$ is a DFA morphism from $M$ to itself.

results.title: Composition of DFA morphisms
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: If $f$ is a DFA morphism from $M$ to $N$ and $g$ is a DFA morphism from $N$ to $P$, where $M$, $N$, $P$ are DFAs over the same alphabet, then the composite of $g$ and $f$ is the DFA morphism from $M$ to $P$ whose state map is $g \circ f$.

results.title: State-separated DFA
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A DFA $M$ is state-separated when any two equivalent states of $M$ are equal: if $p \ne q$, then the languages of words accepted by $M$ starting from $p$ and from $q$ are different.

results.title: The canonical residual map
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible DFA accepting the language $L$. The residual-language DFA of $L$ has as states the left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{y \mid xy \in L\}$ for words $x$, start state $L$, transitions $K \mapsto a^{-1}K$ on a symbol $a$, and a state $K$ is accepting when it contains the empty word. The canonical residual map is the DFA morphism from $M$ to this DFA that sends each state $q$ of $M$ to its continuation…

results.title: The canonical residual map is surjective
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an accessible DFA $M$, every state of the residual-language DFA of the language accepted by $M$ is the image of some state of $M$ under the canonical residual map.

results.title: Injectivity of the canonical residual map
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an accessible DFA $M$, the canonical residual map from $M$ to the residual-language DFA of its accepted language is injective if and only if $M$ is state-separated, that is, any two states of $M$ with the same continuation language are equal.

results.title: States of an accessible, state-separated DFA correspond to residuals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA that is accessible and state-separated, and let $L$ be the language it accepts. The map sending each state $q$ of $M$ to the language of words accepted by $M$ starting from $q$ is a bijection from the states of $M$ onto the set of left quotients $\{z : xz \in L\}$ of $L$ by words $x$.

results.title: Uniqueness of the canonical residual map
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an accessible DFA $M$ accepting the language $L$, every DFA morphism from $M$ to the residual-language DFA of $L$ equals the canonical residual map.

results.title: Arithmetic gate symbols
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The gate symbols of arithmetic circuits are exactly three: XOR, AND and OR.

results.title: Arithmetic basis
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The circuit signature whose operation symbols are the three arithmetic gate symbols XOR, AND and OR, each of arity $2$.

results.title: Boolean interpretation of the arithmetic gates
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The interpretation of the arithmetic basis in the Booleans: on a first argument $a$ and a second argument $b$, the XOR gate computes $a \oplus b$, the AND gate computes $a \wedge b$, and the OR gate computes $a \vee b$.

results.title: Binary gate line
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an arithmetic gate symbol $\mathrm{op}$ and wires $u$ and $v$ of a circuit with $m$ inputs (each wire is an input or one of the $g$ preceding gates), the gate that applies $\mathrm{op}$ to $u$ as its first argument and $v$ as its second.

results.title: Carry wire
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$, $g$ and $i$ with $5i \le g$, the wire carrying the carry into bit $i$ of the $n$-bit adder, in a circuit with $2n + 1$ inputs and $g$ gates: for $i = 0$ it is the carry-in input (input $2n$), and for $i \ne 0$ it is gate $5i - 1$, the carry-out gate of bit $i - 1$.

results.title: Gates of the ripple-carry adder
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $g$ with $g < 5n$, gate $g$ of the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder is the following binary gate of the arithmetic basis, whose arguments are among the $2n + 1$ inputs and the $g$ gates before it. results.title: Gate program of the ripple-carry adder
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $g \le 5n$, the straight-line program over the arithmetic basis with $2n + 1$ inputs whose gates are, in order, gates $0, 1, \dots, g - 1$ of the $n$-bit ripple-carry adder; for $g = 0$ it is the empty program.

results.title: Ripple-carry adder
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The $n$-bit ripple-carry adder is the circuit with $2n + 1$ inputs, $5n$ binary gates, each an XOR, AND or OR gate, and $n + 1$ outputs, built as follows. Write $a_i$ for input $i$, $b_i$ for input $n + i$ and $c_0$ for input $2n$, where $i < n$. For each $i < n$, gates $g_{5i}, \dots, g_{5i+4}$ form a full adder for position $i$: $g_{5i} = a_i \oplus b_i$, $g_{5i+1} = g_{5i} \oplus c_i$,…

results.title: Input of the ripple-carry adder
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n$-bit vectors $x$ and $y$ and a bit $c$, the assignment to the $2n + 1$ inputs of the $n$-bit adder: for $j < n$, input $j$ is bit $j$ of $x$; for $n \le j < 2n$, input $j$ is bit $j - n$ of $y$; and input $2n$ is $c$. Bit $0$ is the least significant bit.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be $n$-bit vectors and $c$ a bit. For every $g \le 5n$ and every $j < g$, evaluating the first $g$ gates of the $n$-bit adder with the Boolean interpretation of the arithmetic gates on the adder input for $x$, $y$, $c$ gives gate $j$ its specified value on $x$, $y$, $c$.

results.caption: Theorem
